title: Models, attributes and the matrix API

blocks.text: 5.3.1 Models, Attributes and the Matrix API

GridCap's planning team runs its selection model on HiGHS through MathOpt. A new partner, a consulting firm, sends its models as gurobipy code and asks whether GridCap's numbers can be reproduced in Gurobi. To answer, someone on the team has to read and write gurobipy: build the same model, solve it, and read back the same plan. This lesson ports GridCap small's selection model (lesson 4.2.1) and its timing model (lesson 6.4.1) to gurobipy, and checks that Gurobi finds the optimum MathOpt found. GridCap is a fictional utility, and its numbers are teaching data.

**gurobipy** is the Python interface of Gurobi, a commercial MIP and LP solver. Unlike MathOpt, it is not a layer over several solvers: a gurobipy model is always solved by Gurobi. That makes it a second, independent way to write the same model, and the API most Gurobi users meet first. Every gurobipy program needs a Gurobi license to start; lesson 5.3.4 explains the kinds of license and how to give the course's runner yours. The course runner has a size-limited license, the one the outputs below come from, and every model in this module stays within its 2,000 variables and 2,000 rows.

Can MathOpt hand a model to Gurobi instead? `SolverType.GUROBI` exists, but in the course's runner it fails: OR-Tools 9.15 cannot load the Gurobi 13 library that comes with gurobipy, and the call raises `RuntimeError: bad_function_call` (lesson 4.2.3 shows the attempt). So this module teaches Gurobi through gurobipy itself.
The Model
The selection model of lesson 4.2.1 on GridCap small: fund projects, each at its earliest start, for the most NPV within each year's budget.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years (2027–2031); $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$.

**Parameters.** $`v_i`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ at its earliest start ($k); $`c_{i,y}`$, what it spends in year $`y`$ when it starts at its earliest start ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$: 1 if project $`i`$ is funded.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} v_i\, x_i
**Constraints.**
On GridCap small that is 40 variables and 13 rows. MathOpt with HiGHS finds an optimum of 22,532 (lesson 4.2.2).
An Environment Holds the License, and a Quiet One Prints Nothing

Everything in gurobipy lives in an **environment** (`gp.Env`): it reads the license, holds parameters, and every model is created inside one. If you never create one, gurobipy makes a default environment the first time you build a model, and that one prints a license banner as it starts. The banner names the license, and it can name the license holder; it does not belong in a program's output, a log a service keeps, or a page like this one.

The Gurobi documentation's pattern for settings that must be in place before the license is read is an **empty** environment: create it with `empty=True`, set parameters, then `start()` it. Setting `OutputFlag` to 0 there turns off all output, the banner included. Every program in this module gets its environment from this function in `grb.py`:

def quiet_env() -> gp.Env:
    """A started environment that prints nothing: no license banner, no solver log."""
    env = gp.Env(empty=True)              # empty: parameters can be set before the license is read
    env.setParam("OutputFlag", 0)
    env.start()                           # reads the license; raises GurobiError if there is none
    return env

`start()` is where a missing license shows up, as a `GurobiError` (lesson 5.3.4 shows the messages). A model is then made with `gp.Model(name, env=env)`, and inherits the environment's parameters: no solver log either.
A Model Is Variables, Constraints and an Objective, Added Lazily
A first model, small enough to check by hand: three projects and one budget of $1,000k.

m = gp.Model("three-projects", env=env)
feeder = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="feeder")        # cost 600, NPV 420
breaker = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="breaker")      # cost 300, NPV 250
trim = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="trim")            # cost 250, NPV 190
m.addConstr(600 * feeder + 300 * breaker + 250 * trim <= 1000, name="budget")
m.setObjective(420 * feeder + 250 * breaker + 190 * trim, GRB.MAXIMIZE)

print("before update:", m.NumVars, "variables,", m.NumConstrs, "rows")
m.update()
print("after update: ", m.NumVars, "variables,", m.NumConstrs, "rows")

m.optimize()
print("status", m.Status, STATUS[m.Status], "| objective", m.ObjVal)
for v in m.getVars():
    print(f"  {v.VarName:8} {v.X:g}")

before update: 0 variables, 0 rows
after update:  3 variables, 1 rows
status 2 OPTIMAL | objective 670.0
  feeder   1
  breaker  1
  trim     0
The four calls map one to one onto MathOpt's:
Three differences matter in practice:

items: **A variable's default lower bound is 0, not $`-\infty`$.** `addVar()` with no arguments is a continuous variable in $`[0, \infty)`$. A free variable needs `lb=-GRB.INFINITY`.

**Changes are lazy.** gurobipy queues every addition and change and applies them at the next `update()`, `optimize()` or `write()`. Before the update the model above still reported 0 variables and 0 rows, and a new variable's attributes cannot be read yet. Building a model and solving it never needs an explicit `update()`, because `optimize()` applies the queue; you call it only to read something back before solving.
**`optimize()` returns nothing.** The result is stored in the model, and you read it from there: `m.Status`, `m.ObjVal`, each variable's `X`. There is no separate result object as in MathOpt.

blocks.text: The plan is right: feeder and breaker cost 900 and earn 670; any plan with trim either leaves out feeder (at most 440) or breaks the budget.
GridCap's Selection Model Ports Row for Row
`build_selection` in `grb.py` writes the model of the first section. Each row of the formulation is one call:
Three gurobipy tools appear here:

items: **`addVars(keys, ...)`** adds one variable per key and returns a **`tupledict`**, a dictionary from key to variable with extra methods (the last section uses them). Its names are the prefix and the key in brackets: `x[P001]`.
**`gp.quicksum(...)`** adds up terms into a linear expression (`LinExpr`), as Python's `sum` does; it is gurobipy's own summation function, and the form gurobipy code usually uses.
**`addConstrs(generator, name=...)`** adds one row per item of a generator and returns a `tupledict` of rows, keyed by the generator's index: `budget[2030]` is the 2030 row, named `budget[2030]`.

blocks.text: Then the solve, with one parameter set on the model:

small = generate("small")
sel = build_selection(env, small)
sel.model.Params.MIPGap = 0.0                  # prove optimality exactly, as MathOpt's EXACT does
sel.model.optimize()
print("GridCap small:", STATUS[sel.model.Status], sel.model.ObjVal)
print("funded:", [i for i, v in sel.x.items() if v.X > 0.5][:8], "...")

22,532, the optimum HiGHS found through MathOpt in lesson 4.2.2, and the module's tests check that the two solvers fund the same projects. `MIPGap` is Gurobi's relative gap tolerance (lesson 3.4.1 defines the gap); its default, $`10^{-4}`$, lets Gurobi stop at a plan within 0.01% of the bound, so the programs here set it to 0 whenever they compare an optimum. `m.Params.<Name> = value` sets a parameter on one model; `env.setParam` sets it for models created afterwards.
Everything You Read or Write Is an Attribute

A gurobipy model reports everything through **attributes**: named values held by the model, by each variable or by each row. `m.NumVars` is a model attribute, `x["P001"].X` a variable attribute, `budget[2030].Slack` a row attribute. Some can be written (bounds, right-hand sides, objective coefficients, names); others are results, filled by `optimize()`. Here is GridCap small's model read through its attributes:

try:
    print(x["P001"].X)                         # no solve yet: no solution to read
except AttributeError as error:
    print("before optimize:", type(error).__name__, error)

m.optimize()
print("model     :", "NumVars", m.NumVars, "| NumConstrs", m.NumConstrs, "| NumBinVars", m.NumBinVars,
      "| NumNZs", m.NumNZs)
print("solution  :", STATUS[m.Status], "| ObjVal", m.ObjVal, "| ObjBound", m.ObjBound, "| MIPGap", m.MIPGap,
      "| SolCount", m.SolCount)
print("variable  :", x["P001"].VarName, "X", x["P001"].X, "LB", x["P001"].LB, "UB", x["P001"].UB,
      "VType", x["P001"].VType, "Obj", x["P001"].Obj)
row = budget[2030]
print("row       :", row.ConstrName, "Sense", row.Sense, "RHS", row.RHS, "Slack", row.Slack)

before optimize: AttributeError Index out of range for attribute 'X'
model     : NumVars 40 | NumConstrs 13 | NumBinVars 40 | NumNZs 69
solution  : OPTIMAL | ObjVal 22532.0 | ObjBound 22532.0 | MIPGap 0.0 | SolCount 9
variable  : x[P001] X 1.0 LB 0.0 UB 1.0 VType B Obj 1401.0
row       : budget[2030] Sense < RHS 8610.0 Slack 70.0

items: **Before a solve there is no `X`**, and reading it raises `AttributeError` with the message "Index out of range for attribute 'X'": the attribute exists, but the model holds no solution to index into.

**Model attributes** describe the model (`NumVars`, `NumConstrs`, `NumBinVars`, `NumNZs`, the number of nonzero coefficients) and the solve (`Status`, `ObjVal`, `ObjBound` the best bound, `MIPGap` the gap reached, `SolCount` the number of plans Gurobi kept).

**A variable's attributes** are its data (`LB`, `UB`, `VType`, `Obj` its objective coefficient, `VarName`) and its value (`X`). **A row's** are `ConstrName`, `Sense` (`<`, `>` or `=`), `RHS`, and `Slack`, the right-hand side minus the row's value: 2030's budget has $70k left.

blocks.text: `Status` is a number. Gurobi's documentation lists every optimization status code; `grb.py` builds a name table from the constants gurobipy defines (`GRB.Status.OPTIMAL` is 2), and the programs print the name:
STATUS = {getattr(GRB.Status, n): n for n in dir(GRB.Status) if n.isupper()}   # 2 -> "OPTIMAL", ...
The codes a program has to handle after a MIP solve:

rows: report a data or rule conflict (lesson 5.3.3)
infeasible or unbounded, not yet told apart; the status-code page says to re-solve with the `DualReductions` parameter at 0 to decide
report a modeling error, a missing bound
use the plan and report the gap, or report the limit

blocks.text: A limit status says *why* the solve stopped, not whether a plan exists; `SolCount` says that. This is MathOpt's split between `termination.reason` and `has_primal_feasible_solution()` (lesson 4.2.2), spread over two attributes.
<!-- practice 1 -->
`getAttr` reads one attribute of many objects at once, in the shape it is given, and attributes are written by assignment:

print("X of a list:", [v + 0.0 for v in m.getAttr("X", [x["P001"], x["P002"], x["P003"]])])   # + 0.0: -0.0 -> 0.0
slack = m.getAttr("Slack", budget)                  # a tupledict in, a dict-like out
print("Slack by year:", {y: round(s) for y, s in slack.items()})

# Writing attributes changes the model: force P001 out, give 2030 another $1,000k, re-optimize.
x["P001"].UB = 0
budget[2030].RHS += 1000
m.optimize()
print("after edits:", STATUS[m.Status], m.ObjVal, "| P001", x["P001"].X, "| RHS 2030", budget[2030].RHS)

try:
    print(budget[2030].Pi)
except (AttributeError, gp.GurobiError) as error:
    print("a MIP row has no Pi:", type(error).__name__, error)

X of a list: [1.0, 0.0, 1.0]
Slack by year: {2027: 720, 2028: 40, 2029: 700, 2030: 70, 2031: 1870}
after edits: OPTIMAL 22613.0 | P001 0.0 | RHS 2030 9610.0
a MIP row has no Pi: AttributeError Unable to retrieve attribute 'Pi'

The `+ 0.0` turns a solver's `-0.0` into `0.0` for printing. Setting `UB = 0` forces P001 out of the plan; raising the 2030 right-hand side gives that year $1,000k more. Both edits are queued like any other change, and the next `optimize()` applies them and re-solves the same model: the new plan, without P001 but with the larger 2030 budget, is worth 22,613. This is incremental solving, as in lesson 4.3.4: one model, edited and re-solved, with no rebuild.
The last line is a preview of lesson 5.3.2: `Pi`, a row's dual value, exists only after an LP solve. On a MIP, Gurobi has no value to give and the read fails.
The Matrix API Takes the Model as Arrays
The model so far was written row by row, the way the formulation reads. The same model is also a matrix: one column per variable, one row per constraint. In the matrix form of lesson 2.1.2, it is

\max\; c^\top x \quad \text{subject to} \quad A_{\text{budget}}\, x \le B,\;\; A_{\text{alt}}\, x \le \mathbf{1},\;\; A_{\text{needs}}\, x \le \mathbf{0},\;\; \ell \le x \le \mathbf{1},\;\; x \in \{0,1\}^{n}

where $`(A_{\text{budget}})_{y,i} = c_{i,y}`$, each row of $`A_{\text{alt}}`$ has a 1 for every member of one group, each row of $`A_{\text{needs}}`$ has $`+1`$ for a child and $`-1`$ for its parent ($`x_c - x_{p(c)} \le 0`$), and $`\ell_i = 1`$ for a must-do project, 0 otherwise. The must-do rows have become lower bounds: $`x_i = 1`$ for a binary is the same as $`1 \le x_i \le 1`$.

gurobipy's **matrix API** takes exactly this. `addMVar(n, ...)` adds a vector of $`n`$ variables (an `MVar`, which behaves like a NumPy array), and `addMConstr(A, x, sense, b)` adds the rows $`A x \;\text{sense}\; b`$ for a NumPy array or SciPy sparse matrix $`A`$. The data are built as arrays first, here as SciPy sparse matrices, which store only the nonzeros:

lb = np.array([1.0 if p.must_do else 0.0 for p in small.projects])   # must-do: x_i = 1 as a bound

m = gp.Model("small-matrix", env=env)
xv = m.addMVar(n, lb=lb, ub=1.0, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="x")
m.addMConstr(spend.tocsr(), xv, "<", B, name="budget")
m.addMConstr(alt.tocsr(), xv, "<", np.ones(len(groups)), name="alt")
m.addMConstr(needs.tocsr(), xv, "<", np.zeros(len(children)), name="needs")
m.setObjective(c @ xv, GRB.MAXIMIZE)
m.Params.MIPGap = 0.0
m.optimize()
print("matrix model :", STATUS[m.Status], m.ObjVal, "|", m.NumVars, "variables,", m.NumConstrs, "rows")
print("x as an array:", xv.X[:10].round().astype(int), "...")

matrix model : OPTIMAL 22532.0 | 40 variables, 9 rows
x as an array: [1 0 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 1] ...

The same optimum, 22,532, with 9 rows instead of 13: the 4 must-do rows are now bounds. `c @ xv` is the objective $`c^\top x`$, written with NumPy's matrix product, and `xv.X` reads the whole plan as a NumPy array. Building rows from arrays skips writing one Python expression per row; lesson 11.1.2 measures what that saves when a model is built from data that are already in arrays.

The other direction is `getA()`: any model, however it was built, hands back its constraint matrix as a SciPy sparse matrix, one row per constraint and one column per variable, in the order the model holds them (each row's position is its `index` attribute):

A = sel.model.getA()
print("row by row   :", STATUS[sel.model.Status], sel.model.ObjVal, "|", sel.model.NumVars, "variables,",
      sel.model.NumConstrs, "rows")
print("getA():", type(A).__name__, A.shape, "nonzeros", A.nnz)
print("budget rows of getA() equal the spend matrix:",
      bool((A[[sel.budget[y].index for y in small.years], :] != spend.tocsr()).nnz == 0))

row by row   : OPTIMAL 22532.0 | 40 variables, 13 rows
getA(): csr_matrix (13, 40) nonzeros 69
budget rows of getA() equal the spend matrix: True

The row-by-row model's budget rows are exactly the spend matrix built for the matrix model. `getA()` is how to check a builder: build the model two ways and compare matrices, or read the matrix to count nonzeros, find empty rows, or look at the range of coefficients (lesson 10.1.2).
<!-- practice 2 -->
tupledict Wildcards Write Sums Over Indices

The timing model of lesson 6.4.1 has two indices, project and start year, and its rows sum over one of them. Lesson 6.4.1 is in section 6, which the course reaches later; section 4 used the same model from lesson 4.3.1 on. You do not need lesson 6.4.1 here: the model is restated in full below, and when this section compares Gurobi's answer with "the optimum lesson 6.4.1 found", it means the first lines that lesson recorded from its MathOpt model, solved with HiGHS on GridCap small:
<!-- unverified -->

OPTIMAL NPV $24,260k
started 27 of 40; 9 later than their earliest year
In full:
**Sets.** $`P`$, $`Y`$, $`M`$, $`\mathcal{G}`$, $`C`$ as above; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$, the start years allowed for project $`i`$; $`L_c`$, child $`c`$'s lag after its parent.
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, project $`i`$'s NPV if it starts in year $`t`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, its spend in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: 1 if project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$.
**Objective.** $`\max \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}`$.
**Constraints**, with $`\text{spend}_y = \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t}`$:

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\text{spend}_y &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}

`build_plan` in `grb.py` keys the variables by `(project, year)` pairs, and the row "project $`i`$ starts at most once" uses the `tupledict`'s **wildcard sum**: `x.sum("P017", "*")` adds every variable whose first key is P017, whatever its year.

m.update()                                   # names and counts are readable after an update
print("x has", len(x), "variables, one per project and allowed start year")
print("x.select('P017', '*') =", [v.VarName for v in x.select("P017", "*")])
print("x.sum('P017', '*')    =", x.sum("P017", "*"))
print("rows:", m.NumConstrs, "| e.g.", [c.ConstrName for c in m.getConstrs()][:3], "...")

x has 80 variables, one per project and allowed start year
x.select('P017', '*') = ['x[P017,2030]', 'x[P017,2031]']
x.sum('P017', '*')    = x[P017,2030] + x[P017,2031]
rows: 49 | e.g. ['once_P001', 'once_P002', 'must_P003'] ...

`select` returns the matching variables as a list, `sum` their sum; `"*"` matches any value in that position, and a fixed value matches only itself. P017 may start in 2030 or 2031, so it has two variables, and the sum is exactly $`\sum_{t \in T_{\text{P017}}} x_{\text{P017},t}`$. The spend expressions are built term by term with `LinExpr.add(var, coefficient)`, and the budget rows from them, as in the formulation:
Solved:

m.optimize()
plan = chosen(pl)
print("status", STATUS[m.Status], "| NPV", m.ObjVal, "| projects started", len(plan))
print("spend by year:", {y: round(e.getValue()) for y, e in pl.spend.items()})

status OPTIMAL | NPV 24260.0 | projects started 27
spend by year: {2027: 8750, 2028: 7970, 2029: 8630, 2030: 8560, 2031: 7720}

24,260 with 27 projects, the optimum lesson 6.4.1 found for this model in MathOpt (lesson 4.3.1 printed the same 24,260 for it before adding its reserve rule). The tests solve section 4's MathOpt copy of the model next to this port and check that both have 80 variables and 49 rows and the same optimum. `getValue()` evaluates a linear expression at the current solution, which is how a program reads a quantity the model never made a variable, such as a year's spend. Lessons 5.3.2 to 5.3.4 build on these two ports.
Summary

items: **An environment holds the license, and a quiet one prints nothing.** `gp.Env(empty=True)`, `setParam("OutputFlag", 0)`, `start()`: no banner, no log, and a `GurobiError` at `start()` if there is no license.

**A model is variables, constraints and an objective, added lazily.** `addVar`, `addConstr`, `setObjective`, `optimize`; changes apply at the next `update()` or `optimize()`; variables default to $`[0, \infty)`$.
**GridCap's selection model ports row for row**, with `addVars`, `quicksum` and `addConstrs`, and Gurobi finds MathOpt's optimum, 22,532.

**Everything you read or write is an attribute.** `m.Status`, `m.ObjVal`, `v.X`, `c.Slack`; `getAttr` for many at once; assignment (`v.UB = 0`, `c.RHS += 1000`) edits the model for the next solve. A limit status needs `SolCount` to say whether there is a plan.
**The matrix API takes the model as arrays.** `addMVar` and `addMConstr(A, x, sense, b)`; `getA()` reads any model's matrix back.
**tupledict wildcards write sums over indices.** `x.sum("P017", "*")` and `x.select(...)`; the timing model's optimum is 24,260, as in MathOpt.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: `m.addConstr(expr <= rhs, name=...)`; `m.addConstrs((... for k in K), name="row")`
the object that holds the license and the parameters; every model lives in one
changes are queued and applied at `update()`, `optimize()` or `write()`
a named value of the model, a variable or a row: data you set or results you read
a dict of variables or rows keyed by tuples, with wildcard `sum` and `select`
`addMVar` and `addMConstr`: the model given as arrays

blocks.text: **Further reading.** Gurobi, [Python API: Model](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/python/model.html) (`addVar`, `addVars`, `addConstr`, `addConstrs`, `addMVar`, `addMConstr`, `getA`, `getAttr`), [Python API: Env](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/python/env.html) (empty environments, `start`, `setParam`), [Attribute examples](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/concepts/attributes/examples.html) (reading and writing attributes, lazy updates), [Variable attributes](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/attributes/variable.html), [Linear constraint attributes](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/attributes/constraintlinear.html) and [Optimization status codes](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/numericcodes/statuscodes.html). The documentation pages are for the current Gurobi release; the runner has gurobipy 13.0.3, and every behaviour shown here was run on it. OR-Tools' [`advanced_linear_programming.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/advanced_linear_programming.py) is the MathOpt sample lesson 5.3.2 ports.
Challenges

items: Build the three-project model with `addVars` and one `addConstr`, and check it finds the same plan.
Add the yearly budget of the timing model with `addConstrs` instead of a dictionary comprehension. What names do the rows get, and which line of `iis.py` (lesson 5.3.3) would then need to change?
Use `getA()` on the timing model and count the rows with a single nonzero. Which rows are they?

blocks.text: Design Note: One Builder per Model, Whatever the API

The selection model now exists three times in the course: in MathOpt (`selection.py`, lesson 4.2.1), in gurobipy row by row (`build_selection`), and in gurobipy as matrices (`matrix_api.py`). Each is written once, as a function from a portfolio to a model, and a test solves them side by side. When a partner's code and GridCap's disagree, that test is where the search starts: if the matrices from `getA()` are equal, the difference is in the solve, not the model.
